content.title: About
content.content: Chicken is the meat of the domestic chicken (Gallus gallus domesticus), which was domesticated from the red junglefowl in Southeast Asia. It is one of the most widely eaten meats in the world, valued for its mild flavor, versatility, and protein content. Chicken is eaten as breast, thighs, drumsticks, wings, and ground meat, and cooked in countless ways.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chickens were domesticated from the red junglefowl in Southeast Asia thousands of years ago.
Chicken breast is lean, while thighs and drumsticks are darker, juicier, and contain more fat.
Chicken is one of the most commonly eaten meats worldwide.
Chicken bones are used to make stock and broth.
Chicken meat can be white or dark depending on the muscle.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Chicken provides complete protein that supports muscle maintenance and repair.

items.title: Rich in B vitamins
items.content: Chicken provides niacin, vitamin B6, and vitamin B12.

items.title: Contains selenium and phosphorus
items.content: These minerals support thyroid function, immune health, and bones.

items.title: Provides zinc
items.content: Dark meat in particular provides zinc, which supports immune function.

items.title: Lean cuts are low in fat
items.content: Skinless breast is relatively low in fat and calories.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Raw chicken can carry Salmonella and Campylobacter. Cook it until the internal temperature reaches 74 °C (165 °F).

items.title: Cross-contamination
items.content: Do not wash raw chicken, and keep raw chicken, its juices, and the tools used for it away from other foods.

items.title: Skin and frying
items.content: Chicken skin and deep-fried chicken add saturated fat and calories.

items.title: Processed chicken products
items.content: Nuggets, sausages, and cold cuts can contain a lot of sodium and additives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chicken can be roasted, baked, grilled, pan-seared, poached, stewed, or added to soups, stir-fries, salads, and curries. Cook it until there is no pink meat and the juices run clear, and use a thermometer where possible. Let cooked chicken rest briefly before slicing.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw chicken in the coldest part of the refrigerator on a lower shelf and cook it within one to two days. Freeze it for longer storage and thaw it in the refrigerator. Cooked chicken should be refrigerated within two hours in an airtight container and eaten within three to four days.

content.title: About
content.content: Gluten‑free cookie is a baked treat made from gluten‑free flours (rice, corn, buckwheat, etc.) and often enriched with natural flavorings, nuts, dried fruit or chocolate. It is suitable for people with celiac disease and anyone following a gluten‑free diet.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Gluten‑free cookies often contain more fiber than conventional ones because whole gluten‑free grains are used.
There are over 30 different gluten‑free flours, each giving the cookie a distinct taste and texture.
Many gluten‑free cookies are vegan when eggs and dairy are replaced with plant‑based alternatives.
Some brands use fermented starters to improve aroma and crumb structure in gluten‑free dough.
Gluten‑free cookies can have a longer shelf life since they lack the moisture that promotes mold growth.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Gluten‑free grains such as buckwheat and quinoa are high in dietary fiber, which promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Low glycemic impact
items.content: Certain gluten‑free flours (e.g., amaranth) raise blood sugar more slowly, which is beneficial for people with diabetes.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Gluten‑free grains often provide thiamine, riboflavin and niacin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Cookies may contain magnesium, iron and zinc, essential for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Additions like dried fruit, nuts or cocoa boost antioxidant levels, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Gluten‑free cookies can contain nuts, soy protein or dairy, which may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Some varieties are sweetened with large amounts of sugar or syrups, increasing calorie load.

items.title: Additive presence
items.content: To improve texture, manufacturers may use additives such as xanthan gum, which some individuals prefer to avoid.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Even without gluten, cookies are often rich in fats and calories; moderation is key.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Gluten‑free cookies can be enjoyed as a snack, crumbled into yogurt, kefir, ice cream, or used in dessert recipes. They pair well with fruit sauces, nut butter or honey.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cookies in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For extended freshness keep them in the refrigerator to prevent fat oxidation. Discard any cookies that show signs of mold or off‑odors.

content.title: About
content.content: Saltine crackers are light, dry biscuits made from wheat flour, water, salt and a small amount of vegetable oil. They have a crisp texture, a neutral flavor with a hint of salt, and are often enjoyed as a snack or as a base for toppings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Saltine crackers were first mass‑produced in the United States in the early 1900s as a long‑lasting snack.
The classic recipe contains no added sugar, making them less caloric than sweet cookies.
They are commonly served with cheese, pâtés, and soups.
In some countries they are called “salty biscuits” or “salted crackers.”
Whole‑grain versions increase dietary fiber content.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: The absence of added sugar makes saltines suitable for low‑sugar diets.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: They provide a quick source of energy through easily digestible carbs.

items.title: Contains some fiber
items.content: When made with whole‑grain flour they can aid normal digestion.

items.title: Contains salt
items.content: Salt helps maintain electrolyte balance, though intake should be moderated.

items.title: Versatile pairing
items.content: Crackers serve as a convenient platform for adding protein (cheese, meat) and vegetables, enhancing overall nutrition.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Excessive salt intake may raise blood pressure and strain the kidneys.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional crackers contain wheat flour, making them unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Although less caloric than sweet cookies, overconsumption can still contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Some recipes may include dairy or soy ingredients that can trigger allergic reactions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Crackers can be eaten plain, spread with cream cheese, hummus, pâté, or used as a base for canapés. They are often served alongside soups and salads for added crunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store crackers in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent moisture absorption and loss of crispness.

pasta-with-tomato-based-sauce-and-beans-.title: Pasta with tomato-based sauce and beans or lentils

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta with tomato-based sauce and beans or lentils is a dish of cooked pasta tossed in a sauce made from tomatoes, olive oil, garlic and herbs, combined with cooked beans (such as kidney beans, chickpeas) or lentils. The mix of carbohydrates, plant protein and fiber makes it a nutritious and filling meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomato sauce is rich in lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that gives it a bright red color.
Legumes provide a high-quality plant protein and can help lower cholesterol levels.
The tradition of pairing pasta with beans dates back to Mediterranean cuisine, where such combinations have been prepared for centuries.
Lentils cook quickly and are a good source of iron, beneficial for blood health.
Legumes can enhance the absorption of minerals from tomatoes thanks to their vitamin C content.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Beans and whole‑grain pasta supply fiber that supports digestive health and regularity.

items.title: Plant‑based protein
items.content: The combination of pasta and beans/lentils provides all essential amino acids, useful for muscle maintenance and tissue repair.

items.title: Lycopene and antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes in the sauce contain lycopene, which may reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease and certain cancers.

items.title: Low glycemic impact
items.content: Legumes slow carbohydrate absorption, helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The dish delivers iron, magnesium, potassium and B‑vitamins.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans, chickpeas or lentils.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Legumes contain phytates that can reduce mineral absorption; soaking or sprouting lessens this effect.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Beans can cause gastrointestinal discomfort in sensitive people; introduce them gradually.

items.title: Added salt in sauce
items.content: Tomato sauces often contain added salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta hot, mixed with the tomato‑bean or tomato‑lentil sauce. Top with a drizzle of olive oil, fresh basil, grated Parmesan or a vegan cheese alternative. The dish stores well in the fridge and can be reheated in the microwave or on the stovetop.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked pasta in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze portions for up to 2 months. Reheat to at least 75 °C before serving.
